chapters.title: Chapter 4: Currencies, Commodities and Managing Risk

lessons.title: Commodity Markets and Input Costs: Crude Oil, Metals and Agri Prices

children.text: Most employees think commodity markets have nothing to do with them, because their company does not trade crude or copper. Then packaging costs jump 12%, freight quotes rise, and the margin review gets uncomfortable. Commodity exposure is usually indirect, which is exactly why it goes unmanaged.

body.text: You do not have to buy a commodity to pay for it. If you buy packaging, freight, paint, wiring, tyres or cooking oil, you are a commodity buyer with extra steps.

body.text: Almost every commodity that matters to an Indian company is priced internationally in dollars. That means your input cost has two moving parts: the global price and the rupee. Crude can fall 5% while the rupee weakens 5%, and your fuel bill barely moves. Chapter 4's first lesson and this one are the same problem viewed from two sides.

body.title: Size It for Steel
body.prompt: Your company buys 1,200 tonnes of steel a year at ₹55,000 per tonne. Prices rise 8%. What is the extra annual cost, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: 1,200 × ₹55,000 = ₹6.6 crore of annual spend. An 8% rise adds ₹6.6 crore × 8% = ₹0.528 crore, which is ₹52.8 lakh. Run this one calculation for your own top three inputs and you will know your department's commodity exposure better than most monthly reviews reveal.

body.title: A Commodity Cycle and the Margin It Eats (Illustrative)

children.text: The middle line is the one worth studying. Input costs move immediately, while selling prices move late, partly because contracts are fixed and partly because nobody wants to be the first to raise prices. That gap is where margin goes to die, and it is a timing problem more than a pricing problem.

body.label: The Clause That Decides Everything
body.context: A customer contract that lets you revise prices when a named index moves transfers commodity risk to the customer. One without it leaves the entire risk with you, however good your procurement team is.

body.title: Who Is On the Other Side of a Commodity Trade

columns.label: Hedgers
points: Have a real business exposure to the commodity
Use the market to fix a price and remove uncertainty
A jeweller locking gold cost, a processor locking soybean, a refiner locking crude
Success means predictability, not profit on the trade

columns.label: Speculators
points: Have no underlying business need for the commodity
Take positions purely to profit from price movement
Provide liquidity, which is what lets hedgers find a counterparty
Success means profit on the trade itself

body.text: Speculators are not villains in this market. Without them, a jeweller trying to fix gold cost for six months would struggle to find anyone willing to take the other side. The line that matters is internal: a company hedging a real exposure is managing risk, while a company taking commodity positions beyond its actual usage is trading, and that needs board approval, not a procurement decision.

body.title: How an Exchange-Traded Commodity Contract Actually Works

children.text: The mechanics are worth knowing even if you never place a trade, because they explain why hedging needs cash and attention:
Contracts come in fixed quantities and grades with fixed expiry dates, so you can rarely hedge your exact requirement. You hedge the nearest whole number of lots and accept a small mismatch.
You deposit a fraction of the contract value upfront. This makes hedging cheap to initiate and dangerous to size carelessly.

Gains and losses are settled every single day, so a hedge that is right over six months can still demand cash from you in month two. Treasury needs to plan for that, and plenty of companies have been caught out by it.

Some contracts settle in cash against a reference price and others allow physical delivery at designated warehouses. Most industrial hedgers settle in cash and buy their physical material from their usual supplier, which is a point that confuses newcomers.

body.title: Find the Hidden Exposure
body.question: A Kolkata company assembles and ships home appliances. It buys no crude oil at all. Which of these costs is least affected by a sustained rise in crude prices?
options: Outbound freight to dealers across India
Software licences paid annually in rupees to a domestic vendor
Thermocol and protective packaging for transit
body.explanation: Freight, plastics and packaging foam are all crude-linked, directly or through petrochemical inputs. A rupee-denominated domestic software licence has no crude content, which makes it the odd one out. Most companies underestimate crude exposure precisely because it arrives through packaging and freight rather than as a fuel bill.

body.title: Aluminium Is Up 18% and Your Contracts Are Fixed
body.scenario: You head procurement at a mid-sized electricals manufacturer in Nashik. Aluminium, which is about 30% of your product cost, has risen 18% over four months. Your three largest customer contracts are fixed price for another nine months with no revision clause. The sales head insists any price increase will lose the accounts, and the CFO wants a plan before the next board meeting.
body.prompt: Lay out the realistic options and what you would actually recommend.
body.modelAnswer: Start by quantifying rather than debating. If aluminium is 30% of product cost and has risen 18%, the direct hit is roughly 5.4% of cost, which for most manufacturers is larger than the entire net margin, so this is a survival calculation and not a negotiation talking point. Then work through five levers. First, hedging: you cannot undo the four months already gone, but you can fix the cost of aluminium you have yet to buy for the remaining contract period, using exchange contracts or a fixed price arrangement with your supplier, so at least the loss stops growing. Second, inventory timing: buying forward physically achieves something similar but consumes working capital and warehouse space, and it becomes a bet if you buy more than your committed order book needs. Third, the contracts themselves: fixed price does not always mean no remedy, so read them for force majeure, index linkage or any annual revision clause, and open a conversation with customers early, since a supplier who explains a cost shock nine months ahead is treated very differently from one who stops delivering. Fourth, engineering and substitution: review whether gauge, alloy grade or design can reduce aluminium content without affecting performance, and check scrap recovery rates, because a one percentage point improvement in yield is pure margin. Fifth, the commercial mix: prioritise the products and customers where you can still make money, and stop chasing volume that now loses cash. My recommendation would be to hedge the uncovered portion of the nine-month requirement immediately, start customer conversations this month rather than at renewal, and take a specific proposal to the board on adding index-linked pass-through clauses to every new contract, because the real failure here was contractual design, not procurement execution. Also flag clearly to the board that hedging fixes cost, it does not recover the loss already incurred, so nobody expects the wrong outcome.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: In India, bullion, energy and base metal futures trade mainly on the exchange known as ___.
body.explanation: MCX handles most bullion, energy and base metals, while agricultural contracts trade largely on NCDEX. Both sit under SEBI's regulation, alongside equity and currency derivatives.

body.title: Build an Input Cost Watchlist for Your Own Team
steps: List your top five bought-in costs by annual value, including freight and packaging, not just raw materials
For each, identify the underlying commodity and whether it is priced in dollars
Write down the annual quantity, so you can size any price move in one calculation
Check each major customer contract for a price revision or index-linkage clause, and list the ones without it
Ask whether the company hedges any of these inputs, and who is authorised to approve a hedge
Set a monthly habit of noting the price of your two biggest commodity inputs, so a trend is visible before it becomes a crisis

body.label: MCX India
body.description: Live and historical prices for gold, silver, crude, natural gas and base metals, along with contract specifications. Useful for checking whether a supplier's proposed increase actually matches what the underlying commodity did.

points: Commodity exposure is usually indirect, arriving through packaging, freight, paint, wiring and canteen costs rather than as a raw commodity purchase
Indian commodity derivatives trade mainly on MCX for bullion, energy and metals and NCDEX for agricultural products, all under SEBI regulation
Most commodities are priced in dollars, so your input cost depends on both the global price and the rupee
Sizing the impact needs only one calculation: annual quantity times old price times the percentage increase
Input costs move immediately while selling prices move late, and that timing gap is where margin is lost
A price pass-through or index-linkage clause in customer contracts decides who ultimately carries commodity risk
Hedging a real exposure is risk management, while taking positions beyond actual usage is trading and belongs to the board, not to procurement

All prices, quantities, percentages and index paths used are illustrative teaching examples rather than market data. Contract specifications, permitted commodities and regulatory requirements are set by SEBI and the exchanges and change over time, so check current specifications before acting.
